title: Arthropod Identification Framework: Pest, Life Stage, Sign & Injury

content.overview: Specialist arthropod identification begins with observable anatomy, life stage, crop location and feeding evidence rather than jumping from plant injury to a pest name. Small greenhouse pests often require magnification, and species-level identification can require expert examination.

vocabulary.definition: Direct evidence of the organism or its activity, such as a specimen, cast skin, webbing, honeydew, fecal specks or frass.
The visible plant response to feeding or activity; injury can support a differential but may not uniquely identify the pest.
A developmental form such as egg, larva or nymph, pupa or adult whose appearance, location and susceptibility may differ.
A pest, beneficial organism or non-pest condition that can resemble another organism or produce similar crop injury.

sections.title: Identity needs more than crop symptoms
sections.body: Stippling, chlorosis, distortion, wilt or slowed growth can have arthropod and non-arthropod causes. Build identification from the organism itself when possible, then combine body form, number of legs or wings, movement, feeding location, by-products and injury pattern. Preserve uncertainty when the evidence cannot support species-level identity.

sections.title: Match the observation method to pest size and location
sections.body: Tiny arthropods can be missed when scouting relies on unaided vision. Inspect the leaf surface and underside, stems, growing points, flowers, media surface and root-zone context as appropriate. Use hand lenses, microscopes, traps or specimen collection when those methods can discriminate the suspected group.

sections.title: By-products and distribution strengthen the workup
sections.body: Webbing, honeydew, cast skins, dark fecal specks and larval habitat can add discriminating evidence. Record where the evidence occurs and how widely it is distributed; do not convert one sign into a facility-wide conclusion without representative scouting.

workedExamples: Fine stippling plus webbing and colonies on leaf undersides supports a spider-mite hypothesis more strongly than stippling alone.
Silvery scarring with dark fecal specks and slender insects supports a thrips workup, but species-level identification may still require expert examination.
commonMistakes: Diagnosing a pest only from crop injury without finding supporting organism evidence.
Assuming every small flying insect near media is a fungus gnat.
Forcing species-level certainty when the available magnification or specimen quality cannot support it.
content.practicalApplication: Build a five-column identification record for a suspect arthropod: organism features, life stage, plant or media location, direct signs/by-products, and crop injury. Add at least one look-alike and the next observation that could separate them.
content.summary: Specialist pest identification is an evidence process. Observe the organism, life stage, location, signs and injury together, use appropriate magnification, and keep the identification confidence proportional to the evidence.
